question: Where should the .gitlab-ci.yml file be located in the repository?

options.text: In the .gitlab/ folder
options.explanation: GitLab looks for the configuration file in the root of the repository, not in the .gitlab/ folder

options.text: In the .ci/ folder
options.explanation: There is no standard .ci/ location — only the repository root

options.text: Anywhere, GitLab will find it
options.explanation: GitLab looks for the file strictly in the repository root. You can change the path in project settings, but the default is the root

options.text: In the repository root
options.explanation: GitLab automatically detects .gitlab-ci.yml only in the repository root

question: What happens if you create a job in .gitlab-ci.yml without specifying a stage?

options.text: The job is assigned to the first declared stage
options.explanation: The default stage is always test, regardless of which stages are declared in stages

options.text: The job is assigned to the default test stage
options.explanation: GitLab CI has a default test stage. If stage is not specified, the job is automatically placed in it

options.text: GitLab throws an error and the pipeline does not start
options.explanation: GitLab does not consider a missing stage to be an error — it simply uses the default value

options.text: The job is skipped
options.explanation: The job is not skipped — it runs in the default test stage

question: In what order do jobs belonging to the same stage execute?

options.text: In parallel
options.explanation: All jobs in one stage launch in parallel. This is exactly why splitting into stages speeds up the pipeline

options.text: Sequentially, in the order they are declared in the file
options.explanation: Jobs within a stage do not run sequentially in declaration order

options.text: By priority, which can be set manually
options.explanation: GitLab CI has no keyword for setting priority within a stage — jobs are parallel

options.text: In alphabetical order
options.explanation: The order within a stage is not alphabetical — jobs launch in parallel

question: What happens to the next stage if a job in the current stage fails?

options.text: The next stage runs but is marked as a warning
options.explanation: GitLab does not continue the pipeline automatically on error (unless allow_failure is configured)

options.text: The next stage runs anyway
options.explanation: By default GitLab blocks subsequent stages when any job fails

options.text: The failed job restarts 3 times, then the stage continues
options.explanation: There is no automatic retry by default. You must explicitly specify retry: in the job configuration

options.text: The next stage does not run, the pipeline fails
options.explanation: Stages execute sequentially. A job failure in a stage blocks all subsequent stages

question: What is the image keyword used for in .gitlab-ci.yml?

options.text: To specify the project logo in the GitLab UI
options.explanation: image has nothing to do with the UI — it is a keyword for Docker images

options.text: To build the application Docker image
options.explanation: image specifies the image for running the job itself. To build Docker images, use docker build in script

options.text: To upload build artifacts
options.explanation: The artifacts keyword is used for artifacts, not image

options.text: To specify the Docker image in which the job will execute
options.explanation: image sets the Docker container image for job execution. This is where all tools will be available

options.text: Only if script completed successfully
options.explanation: after_script runs regardless of the script result — that is its main difference

options.text: Always — on both success and script error
options.explanation: after_script is guaranteed to run always. This makes it ideal for resource cleanup and sending notifications

options.text: Only if it is declared in the default section
options.explanation: after_script runs always — regardless of where it is declared (in default or in a specific job)

options.text: Only if script completed with an error
options.explanation: after_script runs in both cases — on success and on error

question: Which of the following images is most suitable for running Node.js tests in CI if speed matters?

options.text: debian:bookworm
options.explanation: Debian is heavier than Alpine and does not have Node.js out of the box — additional installation is needed

options.text: node:20-alpine
options.explanation: Alpine images are significantly lighter (~5 MB base vs ~70 MB for Ubuntu). node:20-alpine contains everything needed for a Node.js project

options.text: ubuntu:22.04
options.explanation: Ubuntu weighs ~70 MB and contains a lot of unnecessary stuff for Node.js tasks. Downloading will take more time

options.text: alpine:3.18
options.explanation: Base alpine does not have Node.js — it needs to be installed. It is better to use the ready-made node:20-alpine

question: You are creating a .gitlab-ci.yml for a Python project. Requirements: install dependencies, run tests, check types (mypy). Which approach is correct?

options.text: Three jobs: install in setup stage, tests and mypy in parallel in validate stage
options.explanation: Splitting into stages with parallel test and type checking runs is the optimal approach. Fast and informative

options.text: Two jobs: install and 'tests + mypy together'
options.explanation: It is better to split tests and mypy into separate jobs — they can run in parallel and give separate results

options.text: One job with three commands in script
options.explanation: One big job is worse: if tests fail, you won't know if type checking passed. Parallelism is impossible

options.text: One job with before_script for install and script for tests and mypy
options.explanation: It is better to split into separate jobs for parallel execution and clearer results

question: Select all correct statements about the stages keyword:

options.text: stages defines the order of stage execution
options.explanation: Stages run strictly in the order they are declared in stages

options.text: One stage can contain multiple jobs
options.explanation: Yes, multiple jobs can have the same stage value and then they run in parallel

options.text: Stages run in parallel with each other
options.explanation: Stages run sequentially. Only jobs within one stage run in parallel

options.text: If stages are not declared, the default test stage is available
options.explanation: GitLab supports configs without explicit stages declaration — all jobs fall into the default test stage

options.text: Jobs can use a stage without declaring it in stages
options.explanation: If you specify stage: build but don't declare build in stages — GitLab will give a validation error

question: How does before_script differ from the first commands in script?

options.text: before_script can be set globally in the default section for all jobs
options.explanation: The default section can specify a before_script that runs before every job. This is convenient for common preparation

options.text: If before_script fails, after_script still runs
options.explanation: If before_script exits with an error, after_script does not run. after_script only launches if at least script started

options.text: before_script runs faster than script
options.explanation: before_script has no speed advantage. It is just a logical separation for readability

options.text: before_script helps separate preparation and the main task logically
options.explanation: before_script is intended for preparatory steps (installing dependencies, authorization), script — for the main task

question: Your project has three stages: build, test, deploy. The 'build-app' job in the build stage completed successfully. The 'run-tests' job in the test stage failed. What happens?

options.text: The pipeline continues to deploy
options.explanation: By default, a job failure blocks subsequent stages

options.text: GitLab automatically reverts the changes
options.explanation: GitLab CI does not automatically revert changes. This is a task for rollback logic in the jobs themselves

options.text: The deploy stage does not run, the pipeline is marked as failed
options.explanation: A job failure in the test stage blocks the deploy stage. The pipeline finishes with status failed

options.text: The 'run-tests' job restarts automatically
options.explanation: Automatic retry is not configured by default. You must explicitly specify retry: N in the job configuration

question: What is the minimum working .gitlab-ci.yml that is valid?

options.text: hello:\n  script:\n    - echo 'ok'
options.explanation: The minimum valid config — one job with the script key. GitLab assigns it the default test stage

options.text: stages:\n  - test
options.explanation: This config contains no jobs — GitLab has nothing to run

options.text: job:\n  stage: test
options.explanation: A job without script is not valid — the script keyword is required

options.text: image: node:20\nscript:\n  - npm test
options.explanation: You cannot specify script and image at the top level without a job name. They must be nested in a job

question: Your team notices the pipeline has become very slow — every job downloads a 500 MB image. How do you fix this?

options.text: Add retry: 0 to every job
options.explanation: retry controls the number of attempts on error, not image download speed

options.text: Remove the image section — GitLab will work without Docker
options.explanation: GitLab CI works in Docker by default. You cannot remove image without reconfiguring the runner

options.text: Switch to Alpine versions of images and configure image caching on the runner
options.explanation: Alpine images are 10-15 times lighter. Image caching on the runner avoids downloading them every time

options.text: Combine all jobs into one to download the image only once
options.explanation: Combining jobs worsens pipeline structure and removes parallelism. Better to solve the image problem

question: Select all correct statements about YAML in the context of .gitlab-ci.yml:

options.text: Lists are denoted by a dash -
options.explanation: List items in YAML start with '- ' (dash and space)

options.text: Comments start with the # symbol
options.explanation: In YAML, comments start with # and work like in most languages

options.text: Numbers in quotes become strings
options.explanation: In YAML, version: 1.0 is a number, while version: '1.0' is a string. This matters for variables in .gitlab-ci.yml

options.text: The order of keys in a job matters
options.explanation: In YAML dictionaries, key order does not matter. GitLab processes image, script, stage in any order

options.text: Indentation must use spaces, not tabs
options.explanation: YAML strictly prohibits tabs. Only spaces (usually 2 or 4, but consistently)

options.text: An agent that executes pipeline jobs
options.explanation: GitLab Runner is a separate process that connects to GitLab, receives tasks, and executes them (usually in Docker containers)

options.text: A command for locally running .gitlab-ci.yml
options.explanation: While there is gitlab-runner exec for local running, a runner is primarily a CI task execution agent

options.text: The GitLab web interface for viewing pipelines
options.explanation: The web interface is GitLab itself. A Runner is a separate execution agent

options.text: A special GitLab user with pipeline launch permissions
options.explanation: A Runner is not a user, but a software agent installed on a server
